stages.title: METHOD AND THE PRE-1773 CORPORATE STATE
stages.terms: Method and the pre-1773 corporate state: The historical background of the Constitution is the gradual conversion of a revenue-seeking Company state into a centralised colonial administration and, finally, a sovereign democratic Constitution.
stages.mechanism: Read each statute through four questions: who controlled the executive, who made law, who paid, and who was represented.
stages.consequence: Bengal's Dual Government separated the Company's effective revenue power from the Nawab's nominal responsibility.
stages.trap: Plassey (1757), Buxar (1764) and the Diwani grant (1765) supplied political leverage, military superiority and revenue authority. These events are background, not constitutional statutes.
stages.answer: The historical background of the Constitution is the gradual conversion of a revenue-seeking Company state into a centralised colonial administration and, finally, a sovereign democratic Constitution.

stages.title: REGULATING ACT 1773 AND SETTLEMENT ACT 1781
stages.terms: Regulating Act 1773 and Settlement Act 1781: It created the Governor-General of Bengal with a four-member council, subordinated Bombay and Madras in specified matters, and provided for a Supreme Court at Calcutta.
stages.mechanism: Read each statute through four questions: who controlled the executive, who made law, who paid, and who was represented.
stages.consequence: It created the Governor-General of Bengal with a four-member council, subordinated Bombay and Madras in specified matters, and provided for a Supreme Court at Calcutta.
stages.trap: The statute began centralisation and judicialisation but did not create responsible government.
stages.answer: The Regulating Act 1773 was Parliament's first constitutional response to the mismatch between the Company's territorial power and its public accountability.

stages.title: PITT'S INDIA ACT 1784, THE 1786 MEASURE AND CHARTER ACT 1793
stages.terms: Pitt's India Act 1784 created dual control: Company directors retained commercial administration while the British government, through the Board of Control, acquired supreme political supervision.
stages.mechanism: Pitt's India Act 1784 created dual control: Company directors retained commercial administration while the British government, through the Board of Control, acquired supreme political supervision.
stages.consequence: The Court of Directors remained; the Board of Control supervised civil, military and revenue government.
stages.trap: Pitt's Act did not transfer India to the Crown and did not create cabinet responsibility in India.
stages.answer: Pitt's India Act 1784 created dual control: Company directors retained commercial administration while the British government, through the Board of Control, acquired supreme political supervision.

stages.title: CHARTER ACTS 1793 AND 1813: MONOPOLY, SOVEREIGNTY AND EDUCATION
stages.terms: The 1813 exception covered tea and trade with China; wording that all monopoly ended is false.
stages.mechanism: Read each statute through four questions: who controlled the executive, who made law, who paid, and who was represented.
stages.consequence: The Charter Act 1813 ended the Company's monopoly over Indian trade except tea and trade with China, asserted Crown sovereignty, permitted missionaries and sanctioned an annual sum for education.
stages.trap: The education grant did not settle the Orientalist-Anglicist controversy and did not itself create mass education.
stages.answer: The Charter Acts 1793 and 1813 show that monopoly could be renewed even as Crown sovereignty and regulated commercial opening advanced.

stages.title: CHARTER ACTS 1833 AND 1853: ALL-INDIA GOVERNMENT, LAW AND CIVIL SERVICE
stages.terms: Charter Acts 1833 and 1853: all-India government, law and civil service: The 1853 Act added legislative councillors and created a differentiated central legislative council sometimes described as a mini-Parliament.
stages.mechanism: Read each statute through four questions: who controlled the executive, who made law, who paid, and who was represented.
stages.consequence: The 1853 Act separated the legislative and executive work of the Governor-General's council and advanced open competition.
stages.trap: The 1833 Act's equality clause did not produce equal recruitment in practice.
stages.answer: The Charter Acts 1833 and 1853 completed legislative centralisation, ended the Company's commercial character and differentiated law-making from executive administration and patronage.

stages.title: GOVERNMENT OF INDIA ACT 1858: CROWN RULE AND IMPERIAL ACCOUNTABILITY
stages.terms: It ended the Board of Control-Court of Directors system and created the Secretary of State for India assisted by a Council of India.
stages.mechanism: It ended the Board of Control-Court of Directors system and created the Secretary of State for India assisted by a Council of India.
stages.consequence: It ended the Board of Control-Court of Directors system and created the Secretary of State for India assisted by a Council of India.
stages.trap: The transfer clarified the imperial principal-agent chain but did not democratise it.
stages.answer: The Government of India Act 1858 replaced dual control with direct Crown responsibility, but centralised imperial accountability without Indian popular responsibility.

stages.title: INDIAN COUNCILS ACTS 1861 AND 1892: ASSOCIATION WITHOUT RESPONSIBILITY
stages.terms: The 1861 Act introduced nominated Indian non-officials into legislative work, recognised the portfolio system and restored legislative powers to Bombay and Madras.
stages.mechanism: Read each statute through four questions: who controlled the executive, who made law, who paid, and who was represented.
stages.consequence: The 1892 Act widened councils, enabled budget discussion and questions, and used nomination on recommendation as indirect election in substance.
stages.trap: The Councils Acts 1861 and 1892 moved from nominated association to limited scrutiny, not to responsible government.
stages.answer: The Councils Acts 1861 and 1892 moved from nominated association to limited scrutiny, not to responsible government.

stages.title: INDIAN COUNCILS ACT 1909: REPRESENTATION AND COMMUNAL ELECTORATES
stages.terms: The Morley-Minto reforms enlarged councils, introduced separate electorates for Muslims and enabled Satyendra Prasad Sinha to enter the Viceroy's Executive Council as Law Member.
stages.mechanism: The 1909 reforms widened representation by institutionalising religious separation, making separate electorates both a concession and a constitutional warning.
stages.consequence: Official control at the centre survived.
stages.trap: The Act did not introduce dyarchy, provincial autonomy or responsible government.
stages.answer: The 1909 reforms widened representation by institutionalising religious separation, making separate electorates both a concession and a constitutional warning.

stages.title: GOVERNMENT OF INDIA ACT 1919: DYARCHY, BICAMERALISM, FRANCHISE AND REVIEW
stages.terms: The 1919 Act introduced provincial dyarchy - responsibility without control over finance and coercion - and thereby exposed the limits of divided executive authority.
stages.mechanism: The 1919 Act introduced provincial dyarchy - responsibility without control over finance and coercion - and thereby exposed the limits of divided executive authority.
stages.consequence: A statutory commission was promised after ten years.
stages.trap: Dyarchy failed because political responsibility was not matched by fiscal, coercive or overriding authority.
stages.answer: The 1919 Act introduced provincial dyarchy - responsibility without control over finance and coercion - and thereby exposed the limits of divided executive authority.

stages.title: BRIDGES TO 1935: SIMON COMMISSION, ROUND TABLES, COMMUNAL AWARD AND POONA PACT
stages.terms: The all-British Simon Commission reviewed the 1919 system.
stages.mechanism: Its report, three Round Table Conferences, a White Paper and Joint Select Committee process fed into the 1935 Act.
stages.consequence: Its report, three Round Table Conferences, a White Paper and Joint Select Committee process fed into the 1935 Act.
stages.trap: These events are bridges, not substitutes for studying the enacted 1935 text.
stages.answer: The road from the Simon Commission to the Poona Pact converted demands for responsibility and representation into the design choices and communal safeguards debated before 1935.

stages.title: GOVERNMENT OF INDIA ACT 1935: FEDERATION, LISTS AND PROVINCIAL AUTONOMY
stages.terms: The 1935 Act proposed an All-India Federation of provinces and acceding princely states, distributed powers through Federal, Provincial and Concurrent Lists, abolished provincial dyarchy and introduced provincial autonomy.
stages.mechanism: The 1935 Act proposed an All-India Federation of provinces and acceding princely states, distributed powers through Federal, Provincial and Concurrent Lists, abolished provincial dyarchy and introduced provincial autonomy.
stages.consequence: Read each statute through four questions: who controlled the executive, who made law, who paid, and who was represented.
stages.trap: The 1935 Act designed a federation and operative provincial autonomy, but the All-India Federation and central dyarchy never commenced.
stages.answer: The 1935 Act designed a federation and operative provincial autonomy, but the All-India Federation and central dyarchy never commenced.

stages.title: GOVERNMENT OF INDIA ACT 1935: INSTITUTIONS, FRANCHISE AND SAFEGUARDS
stages.terms: Government of India Act 1935: institutions, franchise and safeguards: Wrong: The 1935 Act created universal adult franchise.
stages.mechanism: Read each statute through four questions: who controlled the executive, who made law, who paid, and who was represented.
stages.consequence: Governors and the Governor-General retained extensive discretionary and special-responsibility powers.
stages.trap: Governors' safeguards made autonomy conditional rather than fully sovereign.
stages.answer: The 1935 Act supplied much of the institutional architecture later adapted in 1950, yet its restricted franchise, safeguards and executive supremacy remained colonial.

stages.title: INDIAN INDEPENDENCE ACT 1947 AND THE CONSTITUENT ASSEMBLY BRIDGE
stages.terms: The 1947 Act ended British rule, created the Dominions of India and Pakistan from 15 August 1947, ended British paramountcy, removed imperial legislative supremacy and made the existing Constituent Assemblies sovereign legislative and constitution-making bodies.
stages.mechanism: Read each statute through four questions: who controlled the executive, who made law, who paid, and who was represented.
stages.consequence: Assembly formation itself belongs to the next topic.
stages.trap: Do not claim princely states automatically became part of India on lapse of paramountcy.
stages.answer: The Independence Act 1947 ended British sovereignty and paramountcy and made the Constituent Assemblies sovereign legislatures, but left integration and constitution-making to Indian agency.

stages.title: THEMATIC EVOLUTION: LEGISLATURE, EXECUTIVE, JUDICIARY, SERVICES AND FINANCE
stages.terms: Thematic evolution: legislature, executive, judiciary, services and finance: Judiciary evolved alongside executive dominance; independence is a constitutional transformation, not a simple inheritance.
stages.mechanism: Read each statute through four questions: who controlled the executive, who made law, who paid, and who was represented.
stages.consequence: Mains route: Use a strand answer when the question asks evolution, accountability or inheritance; each paragraph must contain a named Act, institutional effect and limitation.
stages.trap: Across 1773-1947, institutions evolved from corporate control to statutory administration and limited accountability; constitutional continuity lies in structures, not in democratic legitimacy.
stages.answer: Across 1773-1947, institutions evolved from corporate control to statutory administration and limited accountability; constitutional continuity lies in structures, not in democratic legitimacy.

stages.title: BRITISH MOTIVES, INDIAN PRESSURES AND COLONIAL CONSTITUTIONALISM
stages.terms: British motives, Indian pressures and colonial constitutionalism: 'Colonial constitutionalism' means rule increasingly channelled through statutes and institutions without sovereignty resting in the colonised people.
stages.mechanism: Read each statute through four questions: who controlled the executive, who made law, who paid, and who was represented.
stages.consequence: Correct: The Acts primarily managed empire; democratic outcomes resulted from contestation and later rupture.
stages.trap: Constitutional development does not prove democratic intent.
stages.answer: Colonial constitutional reform was neither a linear gift nor a single nationalist victory: British control incentives and Indian political pressure interacted, while authority remained deliberately short of popular sovereignty.

stages.title: CONTINUITY AND RUPTURE INTO THE CONSTITUTION OF 1950
stages.terms: Continuity and rupture into the Constitution of 1950: The 1935 Act is the largest single statutory source of administrative provisions, not the source of the Constitution's democratic legitimacy.
stages.mechanism: The Constitution retained a large administrative and federal vocabulary from colonial statutes, especially 1935, but changed the source and purpose of authority through popular sovereignty, republicanism, universal franchise, rights and responsible government.
stages.consequence: Read each statute through four questions: who controlled the executive, who made law, who paid, and who was represented.
stages.trap: The 1935 Act is the largest single statutory source of administrative provisions, not the source of the Constitution's democratic legitimacy.
stages.answer: The Constitution retained and transformed colonial machinery - lists, Governors, courts and services - while rejecting communal electorates, restricted franchise and imperial supremacy.

stages.title: ANALYTICAL PERIODISATION AND GS-II ANSWER ARCHITECTURE
stages.terms: The best periodisation is centralisation, association, limited responsibility and sovereign constitution-making; chronology earns marks only when converted into institutional argument.
stages.mechanism: Read each statute through four questions: who controlled the executive, who made law, who paid, and who was represented.
stages.consequence: Every paragraph should follow claim - named provision/evidence - significance - limitation.
stages.trap: Periods should be defined by constitutional function, not monarch or viceroy.
stages.answer: The best periodisation is centralisation, association, limited responsibility and sovereign constitution-making; chronology earns marks only when converted into institutional argument.
